abstract.t: This document defines the AI Boundary Declaration Protocol (AIBDP), a machine-readable manifest format for declaring acceptable and prohibited uses of content by AI systems. AIBDP enables content originators to express consent boundaries for training, indexing, generation, and other AI engagement modes via a standardized JSON manifest hosted at /.well-known/aibdp.json. It supports enforcement through HTTP status codes such as 430 (Consent Required) and provides a foundation for consent-aware web architecture.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: AI systems routinely ingest, process, and regenerate web content without explicit consent from originators. Existing mechanisms like robots.txt were designed for crawling and indexing, not for the nuanced boundaries required in the age of generative AI. AIBDP addresses this gap by providing:

ul.li: Declarative consent framework for AI-specific uses (training, generation, summarization, etc.)
Standardized manifest format (JSON) at a well-known URI
Integration with HTTP enforcement mechanisms (e.g., status code 430)
Support for federated and self-sovereign publishing

section.t: AIBDP is designed to work alongside existing protocols — the Robots Exclusion Protocol and the preference-attachment mechanisms of — while providing granular control over AI-specific boundary declarations.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
Additionally, this document uses the following terms:

dl.dd: Any computational system that processes content for training, inference, generation, or augmentation purposes, including but not limited to large language models (LLMs), computer vision systems, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems.
The entity publishing content and declaring usage boundaries via AIBDP.
The AIBDP JSON document hosted at /.well-known/aibdp.json.
A declared permission or prohibition for a specific AI usage mode.
The set of resources to which a policy applies (file patterns, paths, etc.).

section.name: Protocol Overview
section.t: AIBDP operates through the following mechanism:

ol.li: Content originators publish a JSON manifest at /.well-known/aibdp.json
AI systems retrieve and parse the manifest before accessing content
Systems respect declared boundaries or indicate inability to comply
Servers MAY enforce boundaries by responding with HTTP 430 (Consent Required) when violations are detected

section.name: Relationship to robots.txt
section.t: AIBDP complements the Robots Exclusion Protocol rather than replacing it:

ul.li: robots.txt governs whether a resource may be fetched
AIBDP declares what may be done with a resource once fetched
When both exist, AI systems SHOULD honour both

section.name: Relationship to AIPREF
section.t: defines a vocabulary of usage preferences and a data model for statements about them. This document defines an alternative serialization of that model, as permitted by Section 6.6 of that document, which states that "the data model described in Section 3 can be used without this serialization" provided an alternative format defines the mapping in both directions.
AIBDP is not a competing vocabulary. Where the two overlap, the AIPREF definitions govern.

section.name: Mapping to and from the AIPREF Data Model
section.t: Usage categories map as follows:
Preference values map as follows. The mapping is deliberately lossy in one direction, which Section 6.6 of permits:

tr.td: n, unless the conditions are satisfied, in which case y

section.t: In the reverse direction, an AIPREF preference of "y" maps to a status of "allowed" and "n" to "refused". An absent or unknown AIPREF preference does not produce an AIBDP policy.

AIBDP policy keys with no AIPREF counterpart — including "summarization", "question_answering", "generation", "fine_tuning", "embedding" and "commercial_training" — map to an unknown preference for every AIPREF category, as Section 6.6 of expressly contemplates. Where such a key denotes a subset of an existing AIPREF category, it MUST be understood as a narrowing of that category and never as a superset, consistent with Section 4.3 of .

AIBDP's "scope", "exceptions" and "rationale" have no counterpart in the AIPREF data model and are not carried across the mapping. A recipient that understands only AIPREF therefore sees a correct but coarser statement, never a contradictory one.

section.name: Discovery and Caching
section.t: AI systems SHOULD:

ul.li: Fetch /.well-known/aibdp.json before initial content access
Cache manifests according to "expires" field
Respect "canonical_uri" for cross-domain manifests
Re-fetch on HTTP 430 responses with Link header to manifest

section.name: Manifest Format
section.t: AIBDP manifests are JSON documents conforming to the following structure:

dl.dd: String with contact URI (mailto:, https:, etc.) for policy inquiries

section.name: Policy Declarations
section.t: The "policies" object contains keys for different AI usage modes:

ul.li: training: Use of content for model training
indexing: Building searchable indices
summarization: Generating summaries or abstracts
question_answering: RAG systems responding to queries
generation: Synthetic content creation based on corpus
fine_tuning: Specialized model adaptation
embedding: Creating vector representations
commercial_training: Training for commercial AI products

section.t: Each policy MAY contain:

dl.dd: Array of strings describing requirements when status is "conditional"
Array of path patterns this policy applies to
Array of exception objects with path, status, and note
ISO 8601 timestamp when manifest should be re-fetched
Object describing what AI systems this manifest addresses
Object with provisions for specific use cases (academic research, education, etc.)
Object with authorship, creation date, related standards

section.name: Example Manifest
Path Scoping
section.t: A policy MAY specify a "scope" as either the string "all", meaning every path on the origin, or an array of path patterns.

A path pattern is matched against the request path, which MUST be normalised as described in before matching. Matching is case-sensitive. A pattern consists of literal characters and the following wildcards, which have no special meaning elsewhere:

dl.dd: Matches zero or more characters within a single path segment. It MUST NOT match the "/" separator. Example: "/docs/*.pdf" matches "/docs/a.pdf" but not "/docs/x/a.pdf".
Matches zero or more characters including "/", and therefore spans path segments. Example: "/blog/**" matches "/blog/", "/blog/a" and "/blog/x/y".

section.t: A pattern matches only if it matches the entire path. Implementations MUST NOT treat a pattern as a prefix unless it ends in "**".

section.name: Precedence
section.t: Where more than one declaration applies to the same request, they are resolved in this order:

ol.li: An "exceptions" entry whose path pattern matches takes precedence over the enclosing policy. Where several match, the entry with the longest literal prefix wins; if still tied, the first in document order wins.
Otherwise, the policy for the requested usage category applies.

section.t: An "exceptions" entry MUST NOT grant a usage that the enclosing policy refuses. An exception may only narrow. This makes the plain reading of a manifest and its machine evaluation agree, which is the property this protocol exists to provide.

Where declarations from different sources conflict — for example an AIBDP manifest and a Content-Usage header field — the rule of , Section 5.1 applies: a disallowed preference from any source results in the usage being disallowed. For the purposes of that rule, "refused" maps to disallowed; "allowed" and "encouraged" map to allowed; and "conditional" maps to disallowed unless its conditions are satisfied.

section.name: Manifest Integrity
section.t: This document defines no signature format. An earlier revision described a "signature" field, but specified it inconsistently — naming COSE while giving a JOSE algorithm identifier and a JWK key reference, and never defining what byte sequence was signed. Signing a JSON document requires a canonicalisation such as ; none was specified. Rather than repair an under-specified mechanism, this revision removes it.

Integrity of the manifest in transit is provided by HTTPS. Where an origin needs to demonstrate to a third party that a particular permission was granted, that is the problem addressed by verifiable grant credentials such as , which are cryptographically signed, offline-verifiable and revocable. That mechanism is complementary to this one: a manifest states a standing preference, whereas a grant proves a specific party was permitted a specific use.

A future revision MAY define a signature format if a need arises that grant credentials do not meet. Any such definition MUST specify the canonicalisation, the exact signing input, and a single coherent signature format.

section.name: Enforcement Integration
section.t: AIBDP is designed to integrate with HTTP enforcement mechanisms:

section.name: HTTP 430 Consent Required
section.t: Servers detecting AIBDP violations SHOULD respond with HTTP 430 (see draft-jewell-http-430-consent-required):
section.sourcecode:
HTTP/1.1 430 Consent Required Content-Type: application/json Link: <https://example.org/.well-known/aibdp.json>; rel="usage-preferences" Retry-After: 86400
{ "error": "AI usage boundaries declared in AIBDP manifest not satisfied", "manifest": "https://example.org/.well-known/aibdp.json", "violated_policy": "training", "required_conditions": ["Attribution required", "Non-commercial use only"] }

section.name: Detection Mechanisms
section.t: Servers MAY detect AI systems through:

ul.li: User-Agent headers (e.g., "GPTBot", "Claude-Web")
Request patterns (high-volume sequential access)
Missing consent headers when required
Client identification via API keys or authentication

section.name: Consent Headers
section.t: AI systems MAY include headers indicating consent compliance:
section.sourcecode: GET /article.html HTTP/1.1 Host: example.org User-Agent: ResearchBot/1.0 AI-Purpose: indexing AI-Consent-Reviewed: https://example.org/.well-known/aibdp.json AI-Consent-Conditions: attribution,non-commercial

section.name: Federated and Cross-Domain Policies
section.t: AIBDP supports federated scenarios:

section.name: Canonical URIs
section.t: The "canonical_uri" field enables:

ul.li: CDN-hosted content pointing to origin manifest
Mirrored sites sharing a single policy
Federated identity systems declaring unified boundaries

section.t: AI systems encountering "canonical_uri" SHOULD fetch and respect the referenced manifest.

section.name: Multi-Domain Policies
section.t: Organizations managing multiple domains MAY:

ul.li: Host a single canonical manifest referenced by all domains
Use DNS TXT records to indicate manifest location
Verify that a cross-domain manifest is served over HTTPS from the canonical origin

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: AIBDP manifests are public declarations. Implementers should consider:

ul.li: Manifests SHOULD NOT contain private information
Contact information SHOULD be organizational, not personal
Detailed scope patterns MAY reveal site structure
Manifests do not track or log AI system access (use server logs for auditing)

section.t: The protocol itself does not create new privacy risks beyond existing web publication models.

section.name: Manifest Integrity
section.t: Servers SHOULD:

ul.li: Serve manifests over HTTPS to prevent tampering
Where a specific permission must be provable to a third party, use verifiable grant credentials rather than relying on the manifest alone
Validate JSON schema to prevent malformed manifests
Set appropriate cache headers to balance freshness and load

section.name: Denial of Service
section.t: AI systems fetching manifests SHOULD:

ul.li: Cache manifests according to "expires" field
Implement exponential backoff on errors
Respect Retry-After headers
Limit manifest size (RECOMMENDED: 1MB maximum)

section.name: Spoofing and Substitution
section.t: Attackers might attempt to:

ul.li: Serve fake manifests via DNS hijacking (mitigated by HTTPS + signatures)
Inject permissive manifests via MITM (mitigated by HTTPS)
Exploit manifest parsing vulnerabilities (mitigated by schema validation)

section.t: Implementations MUST validate manifest structure and SHOULD verify signatures when present.

section.name: Enforcement Limitations
section.t: AIBDP is a declarative protocol, not a technical enforcement mechanism:

ul.li: Non-compliant AI systems MAY ignore manifests
Detection of violations requires active monitoring
Legal or reputational consequences provide primary enforcement
HTTP 430 responses signal boundary violations but cannot prevent initial access

section.t: AIBDP establishes procedural clarity for consent, not cryptographic access control.

section.name: Well-Known URI Registration
section.t: This document requests registration of the "aibdp.json" well-known URI:

section.name: Media Type Registration
section.t: This document requests registration of the "application/aibdp+json" media type:

dl.dt: Applications that use this media type:
dl.dd: AI systems, web servers, content management systems

section.name: Extensibility
section.t: AIBDP is designed for future extension:

ul.li: New policy keys MAY be added for emerging AI use cases
Implementations SHOULD ignore unknown fields (forward compatibility)
Version negotiation via "aibdp_version" field
Custom fields SHOULD use reverse-DNS prefixing (e.g., "com.example.custom_policy")

section.t: Future versions MAY define:

ul.li: Dynamic policy updates via Server-Sent Events or WebSockets
Per-user consent declarations for authenticated systems
Tiered access levels based on AI system reputation
Integration with decentralized identity systems (DIDs)

section.name: For Content Publishers
section.t: Publishers implementing AIBDP SHOULD:

ol.li: Define clear AI usage boundaries aligned with organizational values
Create manifest at /.well-known/aibdp.json with appropriate policies
Set "expires" field to balance freshness and caching (recommended: 30-90 days)
Provide contact information for policy questions
For content where a specific grant must be provable, see
Monitor access patterns and respond with HTTP 430 when violations detected
Document policy rationale in human-readable form (policy_uri)

section.name: For AI System Operators
section.t: AI systems SHOULD:

ol.li: Fetch /.well-known/aibdp.json before initial content access
Parse and validate manifest structure
Respect declared boundaries or skip content if unable to comply
Cache manifests according to "expires" field
Verify signatures when present and validation is supported
Include User-Agent identifying system and purpose
Consider using consent headers (AI-Purpose, AI-Consent-Reviewed)
Log compliance decisions for audit purposes
Contact publishers via provided contact URI when clarification needed

section.t: This protocol draws inspiration from:

ul.li: robots.txt (Martijn Koster, et al.)
